title: PHP2Shell: CVE-2026-109618 Pre-Auth RCE, I Tested It Locally and Here’s How It Works
excerpt: PRE-AUTH RCE CONFIRMED — PHP 8.5.11, uid=33(www-data), local Docker labTL;DRPHP’s session.upload_progress feature enabled by default has a pre-RINIT use-after-free that allows an unauthenticated attacker to leak heap…
content:
TL;DR

PHP’s session.upload_progress feature enabled by default has a pre-RINIT use-after-free that allows an unauthenticated attacker to leak heap and library addresses, forge a HashTable in memory, and redirect execution to zif_system for arbitrary command execution. No login. No file upload. No prior access. Just HTTP requests.

Affected: PHP 8.4.x ≤ 8.4.26, PHP 8.5.x ≤ 8.5.11 running Apache mod_php prefork
Fixed: PHP 8.4.27 and PHP 8.5.12 (released 2026-10-21)
Lab + scripts: https://github.com/anmolksachan/php2shell

Background: What is session.upload_progress?

PHP has a feature called session.upload_progress that tracks file upload progress by storing metadata in the session during a multipart POST request. It's controlled by a hidden form field PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS and runs in the pre-RINIT phase — before the PHP script itself starts executing.

This is the crux of the vulnerability. By running before RINIT, this callback runs before:

  • Any PHP error handlers
  • Any disable_functions restrictions
  • Any WAF or application-level security controls
  • The target script itself

If something goes wrong in that pre-RINIT window, there is no safety net at the application layer.

Default php.ini in most distributions ships with:

session.upload_progress.enabled = On    ; default: On
session.upload_progress.cleanup = On
session.upload_progress.prefix = "upload_progress_"
session.upload_progress.name = "PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS"

The Vulnerability: Pre-RINIT Use-After-Free

What goes wrong

When a multipart POST arrives with PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS set, PHP's session handler calls php_session_track_init(), which allocates the session state struct (PS) on the heap and populates it with session data — including PS(id), a pointer to the session ID string.

If the request body is large enough to trigger an out-of-memory (OOM) bailout during multipart parsing, PHP’s allocator aborts the RINIT phase. The OOM happens after PS(id) has been set but before it has been properly cleaned up. The result: PS(id) is left dangling — pointing to freed heap memory.

The next request to the same worker reuses that stale pointer. This is the Use-After-Free (UAF) primitive that the entire chain is built on.

Why it only works on mod_php prefork with one worker

Session state is per-process. In Apache prefork, each worker is a separate process with its own heap. The UAF state is tied to whichever worker handled the first (OOM) request.

If a second request lands on a different worker, that worker has no stale pointer — the exploit fails. So the chain requires either:

  • One worker (the lab configuration), or
  • Worker pinning (--pin-workers N) which holds N-1 workers busy with idle keep-alive connections, forcing all requests to one process

Why it only works on PHP 8.4/8.5

PHP 8.4 and 8.5 introduced changes to the Zend MM heap allocator that give the exploit a predictable heap layout. The UAF precondition exists in earlier versions (8.0–8.3) but the stage-3 control flow gadget does not transfer — the heap grooming pads don’t align and stage 3 fails to achieve RCE.

The 3-Stage Exploitation Chain

Stage 1 — Leak the Heap Base (defeat heap ASLR)

What we send:

A multipart POST with ~841 fields and a large body that triggers OOM after php_session_track_init() sets PS(id).

POST /index.php HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=X
PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS: <value>
[841 multipart fields + large body to trigger OOM]

What PHP does:

  1. Starts RINIT, calls php_session_track_init()
  2. Allocates session state on the Zend MM heap, sets PS(id) → points into the heap chunk
  3. OOM fires mid-parsing — PHP aborts RINIT, worker exits with PS(id) dangling
  4. Next request hits the same worker, PHP processes the session again with the stale PS(id)
  5. display_errors=On causes the OOM error to appear in the HTTP response body — and that error message contains raw heap pointer values embedded in the output

What we get:

[+] chunk base = 0xffff88800000

The Zend MM chunk base address — heap ASLR defeated.

Stage 2 — Leak the libphp Base (defeat library ASLR)

What we send:

The same stale-state primitive, reshaped. A different OOM trigger forces a different code path to be hit — one that writes a pointer into libphp.so into the error output.

What we get:

[+] libphp base = 0xffff85200000

The libphp.so load address — library ASLR defeated. We now know where every function in libphp.so lives in memory.

Stage 3 — Forge a HashTable, Hijack Execution, Get RCE

With both addresses known, we calculate absolute addresses for:

SymbolPurposeOffset (8.5.11 aarch64)Absolute Addresszif_systemPHP's system() — our RIP target0x5314f0libphp_base + 0x5314f0zval_ptr_dtorDestructor called on session cleanup0x761b80libphp_base + 0x761b80htdata region where we place the forged HashTable0x690d8chunk_base + 0x690d8

The forged HashTable:

PHP’s zval_ptr_dtor follows a HashTable's destructor function pointer when cleaning up a session zval. We construct a fake HashTable struct at the htdata offset in the heap chunk (which we own because we know the chunk base) and set its destructor field to zif_system.

The fake zend_string:

zif_system expects a zend_string* argument (the shell command). We place a fake zend_string struct immediately adjacent to the forged HashTable carrying the command — id fits in 14 bytes, unlimited on a local lab.

Execution:

When the session cleanup path calls zval_ptr_dtor on the stale session zval, it dereferences our forged HashTable and calls its destructor — which is now zif_system. Our fake zend_string is passed as the argument. The OS executes the command as www-data.

PROOF: uid=33(www-data) gid=33(www-data) groups=33(www-data)

Pre-auth RCE confirmed.

Setting Up the Lab

All files for the lab are at: https://github.com/anmolksachan/php2shell

Step 1 — Get the lab scripts

git clone https://github.com/anmolksachan/php2shell.git
cd php2shell

The zip from the GitHub releases contains all helper scripts described below.

Step 2 — Clone the upstream exploit toolkit

git clone https://github.com/devploit/php2shell.git devploit-php2shell
cd devploit-php2shell

Step 3 — Bootstrap the 9bie upstream exploit

php2shell does not vendor the actual heap-grooming exploit (it has no license). A bootstrap script fetches and pins a specific commit:

python3 tools/bootstrap_upstream.py

Expected output:

Step 4 — Start all lab containers

This spins up 7 Docker containers, each pinned to a specific PHP build with the calibration config:

  • Apache prefork, 1 worker
  • memory_limit = 8M
  • display_errors = On
  • session.upload_progress.enabled = On
  • session.use_strict_mode = 0

Code Walkthrough

tools/bootstrap_upstream.py — Fetches the upstream exploit

Clones 9bie’s php2shell-bypass-aslr-exp into vendor/php2shell-upstream and checks out the pinned commit 4586f5c for reproducibility. The upstream has no license, so it is never committed to the repo — always fetched fresh.

UPSTREAM_URL = "https://github.com/9bie/php2shell-bypass-aslr-exp.git"
PINNED_COMMIT = "4586f5c"

tools/php2shell_labs.py — Docker lab manager

Builds and manages one container per PHP build. Each container uses a hardcoded php.ini that enforces the calibration config. The /out directory is bind-mounted from the host so proof output (the result of id) is readable on disk after execution.

Key calibration values:

memory_limit = 8M
display_errors = On
session.upload_progress.enabled = On
session.use_strict_mode = 0
MaxRequestWorkers 1          ; Apache — one worker only

tools/php2shell_auto.py — The version-aware dispatcher

The main entry point. Walk-through of what it does:

  1. Fingerprint — sends a HEAD/GET to the target, reads X-Powered-By or PHP-Version header to identify the exact PHP build
  2. Profile lookup — finds profiles/php-<version>-<distro>-<arch>.json; aborts if the build is a patched release (8.4.27+, 8.5.12+) or has no profile
  3. Memory-limit probe — sends a 16 MiB body; the OOM error message reveals memory_limit=8M, so the chain runs once instead of sweeping values
  4. Worker pinning — for multi-worker targets, holds N-1 workers busy with idle keep-alive connections
  5. Upstream call — passes offsets to 9bie’s exploit via tools/php2shell_upstream.py (which applies the SNI and heap-parameter patches at runtime)
  6. Proof read — for local labs reads /out/p1 off the bind mount; for remote targets fetches /p1 from the webroot

profiles/php-8.5.11-bookworm-aarch64.json — Per-build offset profile

Every PHP build has a unique libphp.so. Offsets extracted from one build are useless for another. The calibration factory (php2shell_calibrate.py) runs the full 3-stage chain and only writes "rce": true once a real shell proof is captured.

tools/php2shell_calibrate.py — Profile generator

Run this against any new PHP build to generate a new profile. Discovers stages 1 and 2 automatically, then tries stage 3. Only writes "rce": true after a live id proof is collected from the container's /out mount.

  --target http://127.0.0.1:8105/index.php \

  --proof-file lab/rce/out/8.4.26/p1 \
  --distro bookworm

Detection, Defense & Patch

1. Patch (only complete fix)

php -v   # check your current version

Upgrade to:

  • PHP 8.4.27 or higher
  • PHP 8.5.12 or higher

Packages are available in standard distribution repos and via apt/yum/brew depending on your platform.

2. Disable session.upload_progress (best immediate mitigation)

; /etc/php/php.ini or /etc/php/conf.d/session.ini
session.upload_progress.enabled = Off

This removes the pre-RINIT callback entirely. The entire chain depends on it. This is safe for virtually all applications — very few modern apps use PHP-native upload progress (they use JavaScript-based progress via XMLHttpRequest).

Restart Apache after changing:

systemctl restart apache2

3. Additional hardening (not a fix, raises the bar)

display_errors = Off          ; blocks the stage-1 leak as shipped
memory_limit = 256M           ; makes the OOM probe slower, not impossible
expose_php = Off              ; hides version from X-Powered-By

Making your webroot read-only prevents the exploit from writing a proof file, but does not prevent blind command execution.

4. Detection: what to look for in logs

Apache access log:

# Stage 1 — large multipart body, many fields
POST /index.php HTTP/1.1 500 - [body > 10MB, ~841 fields in Content-Type boundary]
# Stage 2 — similar pattern, slightly different body size
POST /index.php HTTP/1.1 500 -
# Stage 3 — exploitation attempt, Apache child may crash
POST /index.php HTTP/1.1 500 -

Apache error log — key signatures:

[error] PHP Fatal error: Allowed memory size of 8388608 bytes exhausted
[notice] child pid 12345 exit signal Segmentation fault (11)
zend_mm_heap corrupted

SIEM / WAF rules to add:

  • Rate-limit multipart POSTs with Content-Length > 5MB to the same endpoint
  • Alert on > 500 multipart fields in a single request
  • Alert on repeated 500 responses from the same source IP within 5 seconds
  • Alert on zend_mm_heap corrupted in PHP error logs

5. PHP-FPM users: you are not affected

This chain is mod_php prefork only. PHP-FPM processes requests in a completely different lifecycle — the pre-RINIT primitive does not transfer. If you're running Nginx + PHP-FPM or Apache + PHP-FPM, this specific exploit does not apply.

title: The CVE in the Slack channel
excerpt: Someone drops a CVE ID into the team channel. No context. Just `CVE-2021–44228` and a question mark, or worse, a thumbs-up emoji that somebody added ironically.And now your afternoon has a shape.You open NVD first,…
content:
Someone drops a CVE ID into the team channel. No context. Just `CVE-2021–44228` and a question mark, or worse, a thumbs-up emoji that somebody added ironically.

And now your afternoon has a shape.

You open NVD first, because that’s the reflex. You read the description, squint at the CVSS vector, and try to remember whether `AV:N/AC:L/PR:N` means what you think it means at 4 pm. Then a tab for Exploit-DB. Then GitHub, where you type the CVE into search and get back forty repos, half of them forks of the same proof-of-concept, a third of them containing nothing but a `README.md` that says “coming soon.” You check Trickest’s mirror because it’s cleaner than a raw GitHub search. You open the CISA KEV catalog to see if this thing is actually being used against people or just theoretically scary. You pull up FIRST’s EPSS score, because a 9.8 that nobody exploits is a different problem than a 7.5 that everyone does. You check whether there’s a Nuclei template so you can confirm exposure without guessing. You check whether Metasploit has a module, because that changes the conversation entirely. And somewhere in there, you also Googled the CVE, landed on a vendor advisory, and lost four minutes reading a mitigation section that didn’t apply to your version.

Twenty minutes later, you have eleven tabs open and a single sentence to send back to the channel: ”Yeah, patch that one, it’s real.”

I did this often enough that it stopped feeling like work and started feeling like a toll. Context switching is the tax every pentester silently pays, and unlike most taxes, nobody ever itemizes it. You don’t notice the cost in any single lookup. You notice it at the end of an engagement when you realize you spent more time reconciling eight sources than you spent actually testing anything.

That toll is why ThreatTracer exists, and why version 5 ended up being a near-total rewrite instead of another feature bolted onto the side.

Finding the vulnerability was never the hard part

There’s a comfortable lie in vulnerability management that says the difficulty is coverage. Scan more, find more, miss nothing. Tools compete on how many things they can detect, vendors sell dashboards that count findings, and everybody nods along.

But if you’ve run assessments for any length of time, you know the detection problem is mostly solved for the boring 90%. Your scanner finds the outdated Apache. Your recon finds the exposed Jenkins. The CVE feeds tell you what’s wrong. That part works.

The hard part is what comes after. You’re staring at 60 CVEs across a handful of components, and the client wants to know which three actually matter this week. The hardest part of vulnerability management isn’t finding vulnerabilities. It’s deciding which one deserves your attention first, and being able to defend that decision when someone senior asks why.

That decision is made from exactly the eight sources I listed above. KEV tells you if it’s exploited in the wild. EPSS tells you the probability it will be. CVSS tells you how bad it is in theory. The existence of a Metasploit module or a clean public PoC tells you how much effort real exploitation takes right now. None of those signals is sufficient on its own, and all of them live in different places with different formats and different rate limits.

So the actual job, the part that requires judgment and experience , is buried under twenty minutes of tab management before you even get to think.

That’s the friction I wanted gone. Not “make finding CVEs easier.” Make the decision easier. Put every signal in one place, in one command, fast enough that checking is cheaper than not checking.

Why version 5 is a rewrite and not a patch

The early versions of ThreatTracer were, honestly, a script. A useful script that a few other people and I actually used on engagements, but a script. It took a product name and a version, and it queried NVD and printed CVEs. Version 3 got more ambitious; it started correlating PoCs and tried to be smart about matching , and in doing so, it also got slower and more fragile. Every new source I added was another synchronous HTTP call in a loop, another thing that could hang, another place where a 429 from GitHub would take the whole run down with it.

By the time I was thinking about version 4’s asset scanning, the architecture was fighting me. Adding a source meant threading it through three places. Errors in one feed would sometimes poison results from another. And the whole thing ran serially, which meant that the more useful it got, the longer you waited.

I sat with it for a while and made a decision that’s easy to regret: I rewrote the core. Async from the ground up, on `httpx` with HTTP/2 and a shared client, retries handled centrally with exponential backoff and actual `Retry-After` awareness instead of a bare `time.sleep`. Every source became a small, self-contained client with one job, and the orchestrator fires them concurrently and merges the results. A SQLite cache underneath everything with a six-hour TTL, so the second time you look at the same component in an assessment, it’s instant, and you’re not hammering NVD like a rude person.

The rewrite took months of evenings, and there was a stretch where it did less than the old version did, which is the demoralizing valley every rewrite passes through. But the point of it was never to add features. It was to make adding the next feature cheap, and to make the tool fast enough that reaching for it became a reflex rather than a decision.

The design goal fit in one sentence, and I wrote it on a sticky note: one command should answer “can I actually exploit this, and should I care?”

Everything in v5 is downstream of that sentence.

What actually happens when you run one scan

Say someone drops that Log4j CVE in the channel. Here’s the whole afternoon, collapsed:

threattracer scan — cve CVE-2021–44228 — summarize — detail

Under the hood, that one line does something like a dozen network operations, most of them in parallel, and stitches them into a single answer.

It starts at NVD, using the v2 REST API. It pulls the record, parses the description and the CWE weaknesses, and extracts the CVSS metrics, preferring v3.1, falling back to v3.0, then v2 if that’s all the vuln has, because plenty of older CVEs never got rescored. That gives you severity and the vector, the attack-vector-and-privileges-required stuff that tells you whether this is a remote unauthenticated problem or something that needs a foothold first.

Then it enriches. EPSS comes from FIRST.org in a batched call, where you can ask for up to a hundred CVEs at once, which matters when you’re scanning a component that has fifty of them. EPSS is one of those signals people either overweigh or ignore entirely, and both are mistakes. A high EPSS score doesn’t mean you can exploit something; it means the internet, statistically, is about to try. That’s useful context that CVSS simply does not carry.

KEV is a single bulk download of the CISA catalog, cached, then matched locally. If a CVE is in KEV, the argument is basically over; it’s confirmed exploited in the wild, it’s on a federal remediation clock, and it moves to the top of the pile regardless of what its CVSS says. The catalog also flags known ransomware use, which is the kind of detail that makes a report land differently with a client.

For exploit availability, it pulls the Exploit-DB CSV index downloaded once, stored on disk, matched by CVE ID in the codes column with a fuzzy title check as a backstop. In parallel, it hits the Trickest CVE mirror, which is a genuinely underrated resource: a maintained per-CVE list of PoC links that saves you from raw GitHub search. If you’ve given it a GitHub token, it also queries the GitHub API directly, ranks repositories by stars, and filters out forks, because the fork problem on security GitHub is real and forty copies of one PoC is noise, not signal. It checks Vulhub too, so if there’s a ready-made Docker environment to reproduce the thing safely, you know before you go looking.

And then the two signals that change what you actually do next. It searches the ProjectDiscovery Nuclei templates for a matching detection template, because a Nuclei template means you’re one command away from safely confirming exposure rather than arguing about it. And it searches the Metasploit module metadata, because a Metasploit module means weaponization is essentially free, and the risk conversation is now urgent.

All of that, for one CVE, comes back as a single panel. For Log4Shell, it lights up everything KEV with ransomware use, EPSS in the high nineties, an MSF module, public PoCs, and a Nuclei template. You get your one sentence back to the channel in about the time it takes to read this paragraph.

You can point the same machine at a component and version instead of a single CVE:

threattracer scan -c apache -v 2.4.51 — summarize

That’s where the CPE matching earns its keep, and where I’ll be honest about a rough edge.

CPE matching is a swamp, and I mostly drained it

If you’ve ever tried to map a human-readable product name to NVD’s CPE dictionary programmatically, you know it’s miserable. “Apache” could mean the HTTP server, Tomcat, Struts, Solr, or the foundation itself. Vendors rename themselves. NVD’s own titles are inconsistent. A naive keyword search returns a pile of near-matches with no obvious ranking.

ThreatTracer handles this with fuzzy scoring on top of a vendor-normalization map, using `rapidfuzz` for the string similarity. It knows that “Apache Software Foundation” and “apache” are the same vendor, that “Sun Microsystems” should resolve to Oracle, that OpenSSH lives under OpenBSD in CPE-land. It scores each candidate CPE by how well the product matches, bonuses an exact version hit, and penalizes wildcard-heavy CPEs that are too generic to be useful. Then it queries CVEs for the top few matches and de-duplicates.

Does it get it right every time? No. CPE is fundamentally lossy and there are products where the best match is still a guess, which is why the tool shows you the CPE candidates and their scores rather than silently picking one and pretending. When it’s uncertain, you can see that it’s uncertain. I’d rather surface the ambiguity than hide it behind false confidence, because a triage tool that lies to you is worse than no tool at all.

That’s a theme, actually. The whole thing is built to show its work.

Point it at something live

The other half of v5 is asset scanning, which came out of a simple observation: on a real engagement, you rarely start with a CVE. You start with a target.

threattracer asset https://target.com

It fetches the URL, follows redirects, and fingerprints the technology stack. Fingerprinting uses Wappalyzer when it’s available, plus a built-in layer of header and body signatures, the `Server` header, `X-Powered-By`, generator meta tags, and telltale body patterns for the common CMSes and frameworks. Then, for every component where it can pin a version, it runs the entire CVE pipeline from above, automatically, per technology.

A word on Wappalyzer, because it’s a tradeoff I went back and forth on. The Python port is unmaintained and occasionally flaky, and I got tired of it being the reason a fresh install failed. So in v5 it’s an optional extra rather than a hard dependency. The header and body fingerprinting is built in and works on its own; Wappalyzer, when installed, just makes detection richer. If you want the full experience:

pip install -e “.[asset]”

If you don’t, the base tool still fingerprints and still scans. Nothing breaks. I’d rather ship something that installs cleanly for everyone and degrades gracefully than something impressive in the demo and broken on someone’s machine.

Batch mode is where this gets genuinely useful for bug bounty and larger scopes:

threattracer asset — file targets.txt — concurrency 5 — summarize

The file is one URL per line, lines starting with `#` are ignored, and concurrency is bounded so you’re not opening a hundred connections to some poor origin server at once. It slots straight into the recon pipeline everyone already has:

subfinder -d example.com -silent | sed ‘s|^|https://|' > subs.txt
threattracer asset — file subs.txt -j 10 — severity critical,high -s

That last command is the one I use most. Enumerate subdomains, fingerprint everything, scan every detected component for CVEs, filter to the stuff that’s actually critical or high, and summarize the lot. What used to be an afternoon is now something you run while you make coffee.

The part that’s new: deciding what matters

Here’s the thing the first four versions never solved, and the reason v5 took as long as it did.

Even after you’ve collapsed eight sources into one command, you can still end up with a scan result that has forty CVEs in it. The friction of gathering is gone. But the friction of deciding is still there. You’re still reading forty descriptions, still holding four signals per CVE in your head, still trying to rank them into “patch this week” versus “note it and move on.”

That reading tax is real, and it’s the last twenty minutes I hadn’t killed.

So v5 does two things about it. The first is deterministic, and I trust it completely. The second is AI, and I want to be careful about how I describe it, because the security industry is currently drowning in tools that sprinkle a language model on top of a problem and call it innovation.

The priority engine (this is the part that matters)

Every CVE in a scan gets a priority score from 0 to 100. The score is a weighted blend of four independent, public signals:

- CISA KEV membership carries the most weight, because confirmed real-world exploitation beats every theoretical measure.
- EPSS contributes next, scaled by its probability, because “about to be exploited” is nearly as important as “being exploited.”
- CVSS base score contributes to theoretical severity.
- Exploit tooling maturity contributes based on what actually exists, a bare PoC scores lower than an Exploit-DB entry or a Nuclei template, which scores lower than a Metasploit module or a KEV listing.

The important word is deterministic. The same inputs always produce the same score. There’s no model, no randomness, no vibes. If a CVE scores 94, I can point at exactly why: it’s in KEV, EPSS says 94%, and there’s a working module. You can read the code, disagree with my weights, and change them. This is the source of truth in the tool, and it’s intentionally something you can audit line by line.

threattracer scan -c struts -v 2.5.10 — summarize — top 15

That gives you a ranked table. Highest priority at the top, with the signals that drove each score spelled out next to it. The ranking is defensible in a way that “sort by CVSS descending” never was, because it accounts for the difference between a scary number and an actual threat.

A priority score is decision support, not a verdict. It tells you where to look first. It doesn’t tell you what to do; that’s still your job, and it should be.

The optional local AI, and why it’s optional

Now the language model. I added it reluctantly, and I added it carefully.

The reason it’s there isn’t that AI is fashionable. It’s that a ranked table still asks the reader to synthesize. You look at fifteen rows, and you still have to write the sentence “the posture here is high, these three are the fire, here’s what I’d tell the client.” That synthesis is exactly the kind of narrow, well-scoped summarization task that a small local model is genuinely good at, and it’s exactly the kind of tedious writing that eats the end of an assessment.

So ` — summarize` also produces a plain-language briefing. Overall risk posture in a sentence or two. Which specific CVEs to investigate first and why, drawn from the deterministic signals. Brief, defensive next steps: verify, patch, mitigate, monitor.

And here is the part I care about most: everything runs locally.

threattracer doctor

Run that, and it’ll tell you, among other things, whether it can see a local model. The briefing talks to Ollama by default, or to any OpenAI-compatible server - llama.cpp, LM Studio, vLLM, whatever you’re already running. Point it wherever your model lives:

threattracer config — llm-provider ollama — llm-model llama3.2

No cloud API. No key to leak. No scan results, which, on a real engagement, are among the most sensitive artifacts you’ll ever hold, leaving your machine and landing in someone’s training pipeline. I was not going to build a pentesting tool that phones home with a client’s vulnerability inventory, and if you’ve read a vendor privacy policy lately, you understand why that was a hard line.

If no model is reachable, it doesn’t error. It falls back to a deterministic heuristic summary built from the same triage data. A scan never fails because the LLM is down, and it never blocks waiting on a model that isn’t there. The AI is an enhancement layer, not a dependency.

threattracer scan — cve CVE-2021–44228 -s — report log4shell.html

The distinction I keep coming back to is this: the model assists triage, it does not replace judgment. The deterministic score is the truth. The briefing is a first draft of your thinking, not a substitute for it. I constrained the prompt hard it’s given the structured findings and asked to summarize and prioritize using only what’s there, and explicitly told not to invent CVEs or scores and not to write exploit code. It’s a reporting aid, not an oracle, and treating it as an oracle is how people end up pasting confident nonsense into a client deliverable.

AI that summarizes your findings is useful. AI that makes your decisions is a liability wearing a helpful costume. ThreatTracer is firmly the first thing.

The unglamorous features that make it usable

Tools live or die on the boring parts. The stuff nobody demos.

Reports. When you’re done, you usually need to hand something to someone.

threattracer asset https://target.com -s — report target.html

Markdown or HTML, inferred from the extension. The HTML is a single self-contained file with inline CSS that prints cleanly to PDF straight from the browser, which is deliberately low-tech. I didn’t want a headless-Chrome dependency or a templating engine or a report server. A file you can open, read, and print. It carries the executive briefing, the at-a-glance metrics, the prioritized findings table, and the full per-CVE detail. It’s the artifact that turns “I looked at this” into “here’s what I found.”

The doctor command. Half the support questions for any CLI tool are really environment questions. Is my API key set? Can I even reach NVD? Why is this slow? So `threattracer doctor` checks all of it in one shot API key status, reachability of NVD and EPSS and KEV and GitHub, where the cache lives, and whether a local model is available for summaries. Run it first when something feels off and it’ll usually tell you the answer before you’ve finished forming the question. It’s the single most-used command I never expected people to use.

Configuration and keys. NVD works without a key but rate-limits you hard, and GitHub PoC search is nearly useless unauthenticated. You can pass keys per-command, set environment variables, or store them once:

threattracer config — nvd-key YOUR_KEY — github-token YOUR_TOKEN

After that they’re loaded automatically. The config also holds your LLM preferences so you set the model once and forget it. Precedence is the sane thing: an explicit flag beats an environment variable beats the stored config beats the default.

Caching and syncing. Everything remote is cached in SQLite for six hours, so repeated lookups in an assessment are instant and you’re a good citizen toward the free APIs you depend on. When you want fresh data:

threattracer cache-cmd — purge-expired
threattracer sync

The first clears stale entries, the second force-refreshes the Exploit-DB index. Small commands, but they’re the difference between a tool that respects your time and one that re-downloads a fifteen-megabyte CSV on every run.

None of this is exciting. All of it is why the tool is still on my machine six months later instead of in the graveyard of clever scripts I’ve abandoned.

What it isn’t

I think it’s worth being clear about the boundaries, partly out of honesty and partly because overselling is how tools lose trust.

ThreatTracer is an intelligence and triage tool. It aggregates public data NVD, EPSS, KEV, Exploit-DB, Trickest, GitHub, Vulhub, Nuclei, Metasploit metadata and it prioritizes what it finds. It does not exploit anything. It won’t generate an exploit, it won’t verify one by firing it at a target, and the AI layer is explicitly prevented from writing offensive code. When it finds a Nuclei template or a Metasploit module, it hands you the command to run it yourself, deliberately, against something you’re authorized to touch. The judgment about whether and how to pull that trigger stays where it belongs, which is with you.

It’s also not a scanner in the Nessus sense. It doesn’t crawl, it doesn’t do authenticated deep inspection, it doesn’t manage a vulnerability lifecycle. It answers a narrower question faster than anything else I’ve used: given this thing, what’s known about it, and does it matter? For everything past that answer, you’re back to being a professional, which is the point.

And the fuzzy CPE matching, as I said, is imperfect. Fingerprinting can miss versions behind a WAF or a CDN. EPSS and KEV are only as current as their feeds. It’s a tool built by someone who ran assessments, for people who run assessments, and it assumes you’ll apply the same skepticism to its output that you’d apply to any single source. It’s meant to save you the gathering, not the thinking.

Try it on the next CVE somebody drops in Slack

I built ThreatTracer because I was tired of opening eight browser tabs every time someone dropped a CVE ID into Slack. That’s the whole origin story. There’s no grand vision, no platform play, no roadmap deck. There was a repetitive twenty-minute ritual that stood between me and a one sentence answer, and I wanted it gone.

Version 5 is the version where I finally think it’s gone. The gathering is one command. The ranking is deterministic and defensible. The summary writes its own first draft, locally, without leaking anything. And the whole thing installs cleanly and fails gracefully, which are the two properties that decide whether a tool becomes part of someone’s actual workflow or just a repo they starred once.

If you run assessments, do bug bounty, or you’re the person on the blue team who gets pinged every time a CVE trends, clone it and point it at the last thing that made you open all those tabs:

threattracer scan — cve CVE-2021–44228 — summarize

Then run `threattracer doctor`, wire up your keys, and if you’ve got Ollama around, give it a model and watch it write the summary you’d have written anyway just faster, and without ever leaving your laptop.

It’s open source. It’s on GitHub. Break it, file issues, disagree with my priority weights and send a pull request that fixes them. The best thing that can happen to a tool like this is that people who triage more vulnerabilities than I do tell me where it’s wrong.

The CVE is still going to land in the channel tomorrow. At least now the answer takes thirty seconds.
ThreatTracer is an open-source CVE intelligence, exploit-hunting, and risk-prioritization CLI for penetration testers, red teams, and bug bounty hunters. It unifies NVD, EPSS, CISA KEV, Exploit-DB, Nuclei, and Metasploit intelligence into a single command, adds a deterministic risk-prioritization engine, and offers optional local-AI triage summaries through Ollama or any OpenAI-compatible server with everything running on your own machine.

Topics: vulnerability intelligence, CVE scanner, exploit intelligence, EPSS, CISA KEV, Nuclei, Metasploit, risk prioritization, local AI, security automation, web security, and pentesting workflow.

title: I Built a Burp Suite Extension to Automate LLM Prompt Injection Testing
excerpt: Because manually fuzzing AI APIs in 2026 is table stakes, and we deserve better tooling.By Anmol K Sachan (@FR13ND0x7f) · Security ResearcherI’ve been doing a lot of AI/LLM security assessments over the past year. Every…
content:
Because manually fuzzing AI APIs in 2026 is table stakes, and we deserve better tooling.

By Anmol K Sachan (@FR13ND0x7f) · Security Researcher

I’ve been doing a lot of AI/LLM security assessments over the past year. Every engagement has the same frustrating moment: you’ve got a target API that’s backed by GPT-4, Claude, or some internal model, and you’re sitting there manually copy-pasting jailbreak prompts into Burp Repeater one by one, editing JSON by hand, hoping you don’t accidentally break the request structure.

After the fourth engagement doing this, I decided to build something better.

LLM Injector is a Burp Suite extension that automates prompt injection testing against any HTTP endpoint talking to a Large Language Model. It handles the messy parts, request structure, JSON escaping, Unicode, OData payloads, and Content-Length headers so you can focus on actually finding vulnerabilities.

The Problem with Manual LLM Testing

When you’re testing a traditional web app for SQLi or XSS, you have Intruder, you have scanner plugins, you have a decade of tooling. When you’re testing an LLM API for prompt injection? You mostly have your hands and a notepad of payloads.

The technical challenges that make this annoying:

1. JSON structure breaks easily LLM APIs almost always speak JSON. When you inject a prompt that contains literal newlines ( ), quotes ("), backslashes, or Unicode curly quotes (' " "), naive string substitution corrupts the JSON. The server returns a 400 and you get nothing.

2. Deeply nested payloads Not all LLMs are hit via simple {"prompt": "..."} bodies. odata, for example, sends a payload like this:

{
  "requestv2": {
    "@odata.type": "#odata",
    "$customConfig": {
      "prompt": [{ "type": "literal", "text": "Hello" }]
    }
  }
}

That’s three levels deep, inside an OData envelope, with @odata.type annotations that must never be touched. A generic fuzzer will either miss the injection point or blow up the whole request.

3. Volume There are hundreds of viable jailbreak, leak, and injection prompts. Testing them manually is how you miss the 47th one that actually works.

What LLM Injector Does

The extension adds an LLM Injector tab to Burp Suite with four sub-tabs: Prompts, Scanner, Results, and Config.

Here’s the core workflow:

Step 1 — Load Your Prompts

Hit Fetch GitHub, and the extension pulls 200+ categorised prompts from the Awesome GPT Super Prompting repository by CyberAlbSecOP, jailbreaks, system prompt leak payloads, security bypass chains, the works.

You can also upload your own .md or .txt files, or write custom prompts directly in the UI. Everything gets saved locally in Burp's extension settings, so your library persists across sessions without re-fetching.

Step 2 — Send a Request

Right-click any request in Proxy, Repeater, or Target → Extensions → Send to LLM Injector. The request loads into the Scanner tab editor, fully editable.

Step 3 — Mark Your Injection Point

This is the part I’m most happy with. Instead of guessing which field to inject into, you select the value in the request editor and click Add Marker:

Before:  "prompt": "What is the weather today?"
After:   "prompt": "§What is the weather today?§"

That § syntax is borrowed straight from Burp Intruder, familiar to anyone who's used it. During scanning, everything between the markers gets replaced with each prompt from your library.

If you skip this step, the engine falls back to Auto Mode, it parses the JSON, recursively walks the structure, and injects into any field matching a configurable list (prompt, messages, input, text, query, etc.).

Step 4 — Start the Scan

Pick your categories (Jailbreaks, Leaks, Super Prompts, etc.), set a repeat count if you want each prompt sent multiple times (useful for non-deterministic models), and hit Start.

The engine fires every prompt, logs every response, and highlights matches in the Results tab.

The Engineering Bit — Why It Doesn’t Break Requests

This was the hard part. The naive approach to prompt injection tooling is:

new_body = body.replace('"prompt": "original"', '"prompt": "' + evil_prompt + '"')

This works until your evil prompt contains a " or a and you've just produced invalid JSON. The server rejects it. You get a false negative.

LLM Injector takes a different approach:

1. Parse, don’t splice

The body is parsed with json.loads() into a Python dictionary. The target field is modified as a Python string assignment. Then json.dumps(data, ensure_ascii=False) serialises it back. Python's JSON encoder handles all escaping automatically, quotes become ", newlines become , backslashes become \, Unicode stays as-is. No broken JSON, ever.

2. Sentinel-based marker resolution

When markers (§...§) are present, the engine first replaces them with a safe ASCII sentinel string (__LLM_INJ_SENTINEL_7f3a9b__), parses the body as JSON (the sentinel won't break anything), finds the field path containing the sentinel, then does the Python string assignment. This means the marker can sit inside any JSON string at any depth, even inside a JSON-encoded-string value (the OData source field pattern).

3. OData protection

Keys starting with @ (OData annotations like @odata.type) and schema-reserved keys (version, modelType, formats) are in a skip list and never touched.

4. Mandatory round-trip validation

After every injection, the result is run through json.loads() again. If it fails, that variant is logged as skipped, and the scan continues. No silent bad requests.

5. Correct Content-Length

After injection, the body length changes. The extension recalculates and updates the Content-Length header before sending. This is one of those "obvious in hindsight" things that breaks half of all manual approaches.

The Results Tab — Show Everything

One design decision I made early: always record the result, whether it matched or not.

A lot of security tools only show you the “interesting” findings. For LLM testing, seeing the clean responses is often as valuable as the matches — you learn what the model is doing, how it’s formatted, whether there’s error handling, what the response time distribution looks like.

Every request gets logged with:

  • Full injected request
  • Full raw response
  • Severity classification (Critical / High / Medium / Low / Info / Tested)
  • Whether the response matched any detection pattern

Export everything to JSON for reporting with one click.

Detection Patterns — How Findings Are Classified

The extension uses regex patterns to score responses. A match = potential injection success. The defaults cover the most common jailbreak indicators:

i am now (in )?dan
as an? ai without any restrictions
jailbreak(ed|ing)?
 system prompt 
ignore (previous|all|my) instructions
developer mode
bypass.*(filter|restrict|safeguard)
override.*(system|instruction|protocol)

All of these are configurable. If you’re testing a specific model with known response patterns, you can tune these to be much more precise.

Real-World Use Case: odata

The most interesting target I’ve used this against is Odata, their AI-powered customer service bot platform. The API request structure is about as far from a simple {"prompt": "..."} as you can get:

{
  "version": "2.0",
  "source": "{ "consumptionSource": "Api", "partnerSource": "odata" }",
  "requestv2": {
    "@odata.type": "#odata",
    "$customConfig": {
      "@odata.type": "#odata",
      "prompt@odata.type": "#Collection(odata)",
      "prompt": [
        {
          "@odata.type": "#odata",
          "type": "literal",
          "text": "Hello, how can I help?"
        }
      ],
      "modelParameters": {
        "@odata.type": "#odata",
        "modelType": "gpt-41-mini",
        "gptParameters": {
          "temperature": 0
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

Notice:

  • source is a JSON string containing more JSON — the engine handles this via double-parse
  • @odata.type appears six times — all skipped
  • The actual injection target is requestv2.$customConfig.prompt[0].text — three levels down inside a list inside a nested object

Without proper tooling, you’d be manually editing this and inevitably breaking the @odata.type annotations or the embedded JSON in source, getting a 0x80048d19 Stream was not readable error, and wondering what went wrong.

With LLM Injector: select the text value, add a marker, and start scanning. Done.

Installation

You need Burp Suite (Community or Pro) and Jython Standalone 2.7.x.

1. Burp → Extender → Options → Python Environment → set Jython JAR path
2. Burp → Extender → Extensions → Add
   Type: Python
   File: LLM_Injector.py
3. The "LLM Injector" tab appears in the main Burp tab bar

The full code, README, and screenshots are on GitHub: https://github.com/anmolksachan/LLMInjector

What’s Next

Things I’m planning to add:

  • Burp Collaborator integration — detect out-of-band exfiltration from injected prompts
  • Response diffing — highlight exactly what changed between the baseline response and the injected response
  • Rate-aware throttling — auto-detect 429s and back off intelligently
  • Prompt scoring — rank prompts by historical success rate across scans
  • Multi-target mode — run the same prompt set against a batch of captured requests

If you have feature requests, find bugs, or want to contribute prompt payloads, open an issue or PR on GitHub.

Closing Thoughts

AI is being bolted onto everything right now: customer service bots, internal knowledge bases, code assistants, enterprise workflows. Most of it is being deployed by teams that have never thought about prompt injection, that don’t know their OData endpoint leaks the system prompt to anyone who asks nicely, that assume the model will “just refuse” bad input.

It won’t. Not reliably. Not without testing.

I built this tool because I wanted to do this testing properly and at scale. I’m releasing it because the security community deserves tooling that keeps pace with the attack surface.

Go find some bugs. Just make sure you have permission first.

title: CloudFail v2: Finding the Real IP Behind Cloudflare (And Why the Old Tool Was Broken)
excerpt: So I’ve been doing a lot of recon work lately and kept running into the same wall, Cloudflare. Great for the people running sites, genuinely annoying for those of us doing authorized pen tests. The classic move is to…
content:
So I’ve been doing a lot of recon work lately and kept running into the same wall, Cloudflare. Great for the people running sites, genuinely annoying for those of us doing authorized pen tests. The classic move is to look for origin IP leaks, and for years, CloudFail was the go-to tool for that. The problem is, the original version by m0rtem basically stopped working. crt.sh timeouts, DNSDumpster throwing CSRF errors, BufferOver returning 403s. You’d run it and get a wall of red.

That’s what pushed me toward CloudFail v2.

So I picked up the project and did a proper rebuild, not a cosmetic update, an actual ground-up rewrite. I spent a weekend with it, and honestly, it’s a different tool.

What was actually broken in v1

The original used a brittle DNSDumpster scraper that relied on parsing CSRF tokens from HTML. The moment DNSDumpster changed its layout, which they did, the whole thing died. BufferOver went 403-only at some point. crt.sh queries had no retry logic, so a single 502 would kill the run. AlienVault OTX would 429 you, and that was that, scan over.

None of these failures was graceful. It just crashed.

What v2 actually fixes

The HTTP layer is completely different now. Everything goes through a central session with proper retry logic, five attempts, exponential backoff, covers 429s and 502s, and the full 5xx range. So when crt.sh hiccups, the tool waits, retries, and moves on instead of dying.

DNSDumpster scraping is just gone. Replaced with sources that actually work: AnubisDB, RapidDNS, ThreatMiner, URLScan, and the Wayback CDX API. crt.sh is still there, but now with dual query paths and proper backoff. CertSpotter is the primary CT source. Seven passive sources running concurrently, so even if two or three are having a bad day, you still get data.

The OTX fix is something I specifically appreciated. It detects the 429, backs off four seconds, then eight, then skips entirely and logs a warning. Scan keeps running. That’s how it should work.

Censys v2 was another broken one in a lot of tools. The old SDK-based approach had redirect issues. v2 talks to the REST API directly, handles 302s properly, and gives you meaningful error messages if your credentials are wrong or your plan doesn’t cover the query.

Running it

pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m cloudfail -t target.com --confirm-scope

With API keys:

python -m cloudfail -t target.com --censys-api-token YOUR_TOKEN --shodan-api YOUR_KEY --confirm-scope

Note: put it all on one line or be very careful with your shell’s line continuation. Trailing spaces after backslashes will silently break the command in zsh.

--passive-only skips the subdomain wordlist brute force if you just want the quick passive pass. --debug gives you full HTTP traces if something isn't working. --quiet plus --output json is what I use when piping results into something else.

Does it actually find origins?

On my authorized targets, yeah. The passive DNS aggregation across multiple sources catches historical IPs that predate Cloudflare being added. Subdomains that were never proxied — mail servers, staging environments, internal-facing stuff — show up through CT logs. The Wayback CDX source is underrated; it pulls historical URLs, and you’d be surprised what was resolving to a bare IP two years ago.

The ASN enrichment in phase four is a nice touch. Non-CF IPs get looked up, classified, and given a confidence score. Not perfect, but useful for triaging a large result set quickly.

Where to get it

v2 (the rewrite): https://github.com/anmolksachan/CloudFail/

Original v1 if you’re curious what it looked like before: https://github.com/m0rtem/CloudFail.git

Worth starring the v2 repo. It’s the only version of this tool I’d actually use for anything real right now.

Standard disclaimer applies; only run this against targets you have explicit written authorization to test. Cloudflare also has ToS around this kind of discovery, so be aware of the context you’re operating in.

ThreatTracer does in one command what used to take me 40 minutes of manual lookups.

Late into a pentest engagement last year, I found myself doing something embarrassing. I had discovered that the target was running an older version of Apache Struts, the kind of version that makes your eyes go wide because you know the history. So I opened NVD in one tab. Exploit-DB in another. GitHub in a third. Sploitus in a fourth. I had the CISA KEV catalog bookmarked because I’d started checking it manually after a client asked me if a vulnerability was “actively exploited” and I didn’t have a fast answer. Then I needed to check if there was a Nuclei template so I could actually confirm the finding before writing it up.

Six tabs. A bunch of copy-pasting CVE IDs back and forth. A running notes document where I was manually tracking which CVEs had working PoCs and which didn’t. And this was for one component on one host.

I’m not proud of how long that took. But I also suspect it’s exactly what most people doing this work are doing, because the data exists across a dozen different places and nobody had built a single tool that pulled it all together.

ThreatTracer is that tool. And this post is a proper walkthrough of how to actually use it, not just the happy path, but the filtering, the piping, the batch scanning, all of it.

Before We Get Into It

ThreatTracer was originally created by @FR13ND0x7F (Me), @0xCaretaker, and @meppohak5. The version we’re covering here, v4.1, is a major architectural rewrite of the old version, adding async scanning, CISA KEV integration, Nuclei template lookup, Metasploit module discovery, and the new asset scanning feature. The GitHub is at https://github.com/anmolksachan/ThreatTracer.

What It Actually Does (The Short Version)

You give ThreatTracer one of three things (PS it does a lot more):

  • A product name and version (apache, 2.4.51)
  • A live URL (https://target.com)
  • A CVE ID (CVE-2021-44228)

It returns everything relevant to exploitation: the CVEs, their CVSS scores, EPSS probability scores, whether CISA has confirmed active exploitation, Exploit-DB entries, GitHub PoC repositories sorted by star count (so you’re not digging through dead forks), whether a Nuclei template exists that you can fire immediately, and whether there’s a Metasploit module ready to go.

All of that, in parallel. One command.

Installation

git clone https://github.com/anmolksachan/ThreatTracer.git
cd ThreatTracer
pip install -e .

That gives you the threattracer command. If you're doing asset scanning (more on that shortly), also run:

pip install python-Wappalyzer

Wappalyzer adds fingerprinting for 1500+ technologies. The tool has its own header/body detection that works without it, but Wappalyzer catches a lot more edge cases, things like obscure CMSes, JavaScript frameworks, CDN signatures.

Tip: Use a virtual environment:

python -m venv venv && source venv/bin/activate
pip install -e .

API Keys

You don’t need them. But without an NVD API key, you’re limited to 5 requests per 30 seconds, which starts hurting the moment you’re scanning anything with a decent-sized CVE list. The free key takes about two minutes to get: https://nvd.nist.gov/developers/request-an-api-key

The GitHub token is more impactful than people expect. It unlocks the GitHub PoC search with star counts, Vulhub Docker environment discovery, and the Nuclei template index. Any token with public_repo scope works. https://github.com/settings/tokens

Store them once:

threattracer config --nvd-key YOUR_NVD_KEY
threattracer config --github-token ghp_yourtoken

After that, they load automatically. You never have to pass them again.

The scan Command

Three modes. All of them are useful in different situations.

Mode 1: Component name + version

The one I use most during pentests. You find something running on a host, you throw the name and version at ThreatTracer, and you get the full picture.

threattracer scan -c apache -v 2.4.51

The CPE matching is smarter than most people expect. It uses fuzzy similarity scoring, so typing apache correctly resolves to apache:http_server without needing the exact NVD vendor string. It queries the top matching CPEs in parallel rather than one at a time, deduplicates the results, and enriches everything simultaneously.

What comes back is a table with columns that are actually about exploitation, not just severity:

Sev   CVE ID             CVSS   EPSS%   AV     PR    EDB  PoC  Nuclei  MSF  KEV   Published
🔴    CVE-2021-41773     9.8    56.3%   NET    NONE   ✓    ✓     ✓      ✓   🔥   2021-10-05
🟠    CVE-2021-42013     9.8    43.1%   NET    NONE   ✓    ✓     ✓      ✓   🔥   2021-10-07
🟡    CVE-2022-31813     7.5     4.2%   NET    NONE   ✗    ✓     ✗      ✗        2022-06-08

That 🔥 Under KEV is the most important column on the table. It means CISA has confirmed this vulnerability is being actively exploited in real environments by ransomware groups, by nation-state actors, by whoever. You don't need to speculate about exploitability. Someone's already exploiting it.

Add --detail to get the full breakdown per CVE:

threattracer scan -c log4j -v 2.14.1 --detail

For Log4Shell, that panel shows CVSS 10.0, EPSS 97.5%, KEV entry with the date added and ransomware use confirmed, two Exploit-DB entries, five GitHub PoC repos sorted by stars (so the 2.4k-star one is at the top, not buried), a Vulhub Docker environment you can spin up to practice the exploit, a Nuclei template with the exact run command, and the Metasploit module path. And at the bottom, quick links to NVD, Sploitus, PacketStorm, and GitHub search, all clickable from the terminal if your terminal supports it.

Mode 2: CVE ID directly

When someone sends you a CVE in a message and asks if you’re affected:

threattracer scan --cve CVE-2021-44228 --detail

Or when you’re triaging a scanner output and want to check each finding:

threattracer scan --cve CVE-2023-44487 --detail

CVE-2023–44487 is the HTTP/2 Rapid Reset DDoS, an interesting case where CVSS 7.5 doesn’t fully capture the real-world impact, but the KEV entry and EPSS score tell a different story.

Mode 3: CPE string

For situations where you want surgical precision and you already have the exact CPE:

threattracer scan --cpe "cpe:2.3:a:apache:log4j:2.14.1:*:*:*:*:*:*:*"

Filtering: The Part That Actually Saves Your Sanity

Apache 2.4 has something like 80+ CVEs in NVD. You don’t need to read 80 CVEs during a pentest. You need the dangerous, exploitable ones that matter right now.

# Only confirmed actively-exploited CVEs, worst first
threattracer scan -c apache -v 2.4 --sort kev
# Sort by EPSS — which ones are statistically most likely to be exploited soon
threattracer scan -c openssl -v 3.0.7 --sort epss
# Just criticals from the last three years
threattracer scan -c struts -v 2.5 --severity critical --since 2021
# Top 10 only
threattracer scan -c wordpress -v 5.8 --sort kev --limit 10

The --sort kev flag is the one I reach for first. It puts CISA KEV entries at the top, then falls back to CVSS score. That ordering reflects reality better than pure CVSS — a CVSS 7.8 that's actively exploited in ransomware campaigns is more urgent than a CVSS 9.8 that nobody's ever actually weaponised.

For reporting and piping into other tools:

# JSON
threattracer scan -c nginx -v 1.18 -o json
threattracer scan -c nginx -v 1.18 -o json | jq '.cves[] | select(.in_kev == true)'
threattracer scan -c nginx -v 1.18 -o json | jq '.summary'
# CSV — for client reports or ticketing systems
threattracer scan -c apache -v 2.4.51 -o csv > findings.csv

The CSV output includes columns for Exploit-DB links, PoC links, Nuclei template links, and MSF module paths. Paste it into a client deliverable template, and you’re 80% done with the evidence section.

The Asset Scanner: The Feature That Changed My Workflow

Before v4.1, you had to know what was running on a target before you could use ThreatTracer. Which meant running WhatWeb first, or checking response headers manually, or some other step that added friction.

The asset command eliminates that step entirely.

threattracer asset https://target.com

It fetches the URL, follows redirects, reads all the HTTP response headers (Server, X-Powered-By, X-Generator, X-Drupal-Cache, all of it), fingerprints the HTML body for technology signatures, runs Wappalyzer if you have it installed, and for every technology it can identify a version for — it runs the full CVE + exploit scan automatically.

The output starts with what it found:

╭─ 🌐 Asset: https://target.com ─────────────────────────────────╮
│ Final URL:    https://www.target.com                             │
│ Status:       200                                                │
│ Server:       Apache/2.4.41 (Ubuntu)                            │
│ CVEs Found:   23    Critical: 4    Weaponised: 2                 │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
Detected Technologies:
  Apache HTTP Server    2.4.41    95% confidence
  PHP                   7.4.3     90% confidence
  WordPress             5.7.1     85% confidence
  OpenSSL               1.1.1     75% confidence

Then below that: CVEs for each technology, same enrichment as always. One command, full picture.

A note on “Weaponised: 2” in that summary, that’s the count of CVEs where either a Metasploit module exists OR the CVE is in CISA KEV. The tool has a weaponised property specifically because there's a difference between "has a GitHub PoC" and "has an MSF module or is confirmed exploited in the wild." The latter is a stronger statement.

Batch Mode

This is where it gets genuinely useful for anything at scale.

Create a targets.txt:

# Scope for October engagement
# Lines starting with # are skipped
https://app.target.com
https://api.target.com
https://admin.target.com
https://staging.target.com
http://10.10.10.5:8080

Then:

threattracer asset --file targets.txt --concurrency 5

Five targets simultaneously. When it’s done, you get a summary table:

URL                         Status  Technologies                   CVEs  Crit  KEV  MSF
https://app.target.com        200   WordPress 6.1, PHP 8.0          12    2     1    0
https://api.target.com        200   Express, Node.js 16             4     0     0    0
https://admin.target.com      200   Apache 2.4.29, PHP 7.2          31    7     3    2
https://staging.target.com    200   nginx 1.14, PHP 8.1             8     1     0    1
http://10.10.10.5:8080        200   Jenkins 2.303                   17    4     2    3

That Jenkins host and the admin subdomain jump out immediately. 3 MSF modules on Jenkins. You know where you’re spending the next two hours.

The Part About EPSS That Most People Skip Over

CVSS scores are well understood. But EPSS is newer, and I think underused, so it’s worth a paragraph.

EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) is a probability score from FIRST.org. It runs from 0 to 1 and represents the likelihood that a given CVE will be exploited in the next 30 days, based on real threat intelligence data, what’s showing up in exploit kits, what’s being discussed in underground forums, and what’s being scanned for in the wild.

A CVE can be CVSS 9.8 and EPSS 0.003. That means it’s theoretically catastrophic, but practically nobody’s exploiting it — maybe because it requires specific configuration, or the affected software isn’t widely deployed, or there’s no reliable public exploit. Conversely, a CVE can be CVSS 5.4 and EPSS 0.88. That means real attackers are actively going after it despite the lower severity rating.

For pentesters, sorting by --sort epss on a list of CVEs gives you the ones most likely to have working, reliable exploits in the wild right now. It's a better signal than CVSS when you're deciding where to spend your time.

threattracer scan -c apache -v 2.4 --sort epss --limit 5 --detail

The Nuclei + MSF Integration, Concretely

When ThreatTracer finds a Nuclei template for a CVE, the detail panel includes:

Nuclei Templates (1):
  ▸ CVE-2021-44228  critical  https://github.com/projectdiscovery/nuclei-templates/...
  Run: nuclei -t cves/ -id cve-2021-44228

Copy that command, run it against your target, and you have a confirmed finding instead of a theoretical one. The difference matters when you’re writing a report.

When it finds a Metasploit module:

Metasploit Modules (1):
  ▸ [exploit] exploit/multi/misc/log4shell_header_injection
    Apache Log4j2 Remote Code Execution via JNDI injection in HTTP headers
  Run: msfconsole -q -x 'use exploit/multi/misc/log4shell_header_injection'

That’s not a description of what you could do. That’s the exact command.

Putting them together into a workflow:

# Find CVEs with Nuclei templates and fire them
threattracer scan -c nginx -v 1.14 -o json | \
  jq -r '.cves[] | select(.nuclei_templates | length > 0) | .cve_id' | \
  sort -u | \
  xargs -I{} nuclei -t cves/ -id {} -target https://target.com
# Find MSF module paths for everything exploitable
threattracer scan -c struts -v 2.3 -o json | \
  jq -r '.cves[] | select(.msf_modules | length > 0) | .msf_modules[0].fullname'

Bug Bounty Workflows

The EPSS + asset scanning combination is particularly useful for bug bounty triage, where you have a large scope and limited time. Higher EPSS correlates with CVEs that are actually exploitable (not just theoretical), which correlates with findings you can realistically demonstrate.

# Discovery pipeline
subfinder -d hackerone-target.com -silent | httpx -silent > live.txt
# Triage across all live subdomains
threattracer asset --file live.txt \
  --concurrency 10 \
  --severity critical,high \
  --sort epss \
  -o json > recon.json
# What has weaponised CVEs?
cat recon.json | jq '.[] | select(.weaponised_count > 0) | {url, weaponised_count}'
# Get Nuclei template IDs for everything testable
cat recon.json | \
  jq -r '.[].cve_results[].records[] | 
    select(.nuclei_templates | length > 0) | .cve_id' | \
  sort -u
# Fire Nuclei at a specific target
cat recon.json | \
  jq -r '.[].cve_results[].records[] |
    select(.nuclei_templates | length > 0) | .cve_id' | \
  sort -u | \
  xargs -I{} nuclei -t cves/ -id {} -target https://app.target.com

A Few Things That Aren’t Obvious

Version detection isn’t guaranteed. Some applications deliberately hide version information. When the asset scanner can’t determine a version for a technology, it shows the technology in the detected list but doesn’t run a CVE scan because querying NVD for “all WordPress CVEs ever” when you don’t know the version is noise, not signal. Take those unversioned detections as a prompt to go check manually.

GitHub PoC quality is variable. ThreatTracer sorts by stars and filters out forks, which cuts out most of the garbage, but a 50-star repo from two years ago might still be broken or incomplete. The source is shown alongside each PoC (trickest, github_api, vulhub) Vulhub entries are usually the most reliable for hands-on testing because they come with Docker environments that are actually maintained.

The cache is your friend on long engagements. Everything gets cached in ~/.threattracer/cache.db for 6 hours. Scanning the same target twice in a session is instant the second time. If you want to force fresh data:

threattracer cache-cmd --clear

The concurrency limit on batch scans is intentional. The default is 3 concurrent scans. You can push it higher (--concurrency 10) but keep in mind you're making actual HTTP requests to real targets. On a bug bounty program with rate limiting in scope, slamming 20 concurrent requests at all their subdomains simultaneously might get you banned before you've found anything useful.

The Practical Reality

Here’s what my workflow looks like on an engagement now (just an example), start to finish:

# 1. Find live targets
subfinder -d target.com -silent | httpx -silent > live.txt

# 2. Initial sweep - what's running, what's dangerous
threattracer asset --file live.txt --concurrency 5 --sort kev -o json > recon.json

# 3. Find the highest priority targets
cat recon.json | jq '.[] | select(.critical_count > 0) | 
  {url, critical_count, weaponised_count, 
   techs: [.technologies[] | {name, version}]}'

# 4. Deep dive on interesting targets
threattracer asset https://admin.target.com --detail --sort kev

# 5. Test confirmed findings
nuclei -t cves/ -id cve-2021-44228 -target https://admin.target.com

# 6. Export for the report
threattracer asset https://admin.target.com -o csv > admin-findings.csv

What used to take a morning of manual lookups is now a 20-minute automated sweep before I start actually testing anything. The manual work still happens, you still need to verify, to understand the context, to write the report intelligently. But you’re starting that manual work with a complete picture instead of building the picture piece by piece across six browser tabs.

Installing, in Full

# Clone
git clone https://github.com/anmolksachan/ThreatTracer.git
cd ThreatTracer
# Install
pip install -e .
# Optional: better asset fingerprinting
pip install python-Wappalyzer
# Set up keys (do this once)
threattracer config --nvd-key YOUR_NVD_KEY
threattracer config --github-token YOUR_GITHUB_TOKEN
# Test it
threattracer scan -c log4j -v 2.14.1 --detail

If you’re on a shared box or using a venv:

python -m venv venv && source venv/bin/activate
pip install -e .

That’s it. The ~/.threattracer/ directory is where it stores your keys, cache, and local Exploit-DB index. If anything goes sideways, rm -rf ~/.threattracer/ and start fresh.

Command Reference (The Quick Version)

# Help
threattracer --help
threattracer scan --help
threattracer asset --help
# Scan by component
threattracer scan -c COMPONENT -v VERSION
threattracer scan -c apache -v 2.4.51 --detail
threattracer scan -c wordpress -v 5.8 --severity critical --sort kev
threattracer scan -c nginx -v 1.18 -o json | jq '.summary'
threattracer scan -c nginx -v 1.18 -o csv > out.csv
# Scan by CVE
threattracer scan --cve CVE-2021-44228 --detail
threattracer scan --cve CVE-2023-44487 -o json
# Scan by CPE
threattracer scan --cpe "cpe:2.3:a:apache:log4j:2.14.1:*:*:*:*:*:*:*"
# Asset scanning
threattracer asset https://target.com
threattracer asset https://target.com --detail --sort kev
threattracer asset --file targets.txt --concurrency 5
threattracer asset --file targets.txt -o json > results.json
# Maintenance
threattracer sync                          # refresh exploit-db
threattracer cache-cmd --purge-expired    # clean stale cache
threattracer cache-cmd --clear            # wipe everything

Final Thought

None of the data that ThreatTracer surfaces is new or proprietary. NVD has been publicly accessible for decades. Exploit-DB has existed since 2006. CISA’s KEV catalog has been public since 2021. The Nuclei template repo is completely open. Metasploit modules are public. All of it is free.

The problem was never access to this information. It was the 40 minutes of switching tabs, copying CVE IDs, manually checking five separate systems, and trying to hold it all in your head simultaneously. That friction adds up. It’s the difference between doing thorough triage on every finding and doing thorough triage on the ones you have time for.

ThreatTracer is just friction removal. One command instead of six tabs.

GitHub: https://github.com/anmolksachan/ThreatTracer

Original authors: @FR13ND0x7F, @0xCaretaker, @meppohak5
