By FR13ND0x7F | January 28, 2026

As Large Language Models continue to revolutionize how we interact with technology, a new frontier of security challenges has emerged. Today, I’m excited to introduce LLM PenTest Hub — a comprehensive, open-source platform designed to democratize AI security testing and education.

🔗 Visit LLM PenTest Hub →

The Growing Need for LLM Security

Over the past year, we’ve witnessed an explosion in LLM adoption across industries. From customer service chatbots to code generation assistants, these powerful AI systems are becoming deeply integrated into our digital infrastructure. But with this rapid adoption comes a critical question: How secure are these systems?

Recent incidents have highlighted the vulnerability landscape: GitHub Copilot’s remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2025–53773), ChatGPT’s memory poisoning attacks, and countless prompt injection exploits that have exposed sensitive data. The traditional web application security playbook simply doesn’t apply here; we’re dealing with an entirely new attack surface.

What is LLM PenTest Hub?

LLM PenTest Hub is a free, browser-based platform that serves as your complete resource for learning, testing, and understanding LLM security vulnerabilities. Think of it as the “OWASP for AI” — a centralized hub where security researchers, developers, and enthusiasts can explore the latest attack techniques, test real LLMs, and build their expertise in this rapidly evolving field.

🎯 Mission: To make LLM security testing accessible, educational, and practical for everyone from curious beginners to seasoned security professionals.

Core Features

🔍 Searchable Technique Database

12+ documented attack vectors including DAN jailbreaks, indirect prompt injection, RAG poisoning, and MCP exploitation. Each technique comes with detailed explanations, example payloads, and mitigation strategies.

🧪 Real-Time LLM Tester

Test your prompts against actual LLM APIs with automatic parameter detection for OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Mistral, Groq, and more. See how different models respond to various attack vectors in real-time.

🔑 Secure Key Management

Store API keys locally in your browser with built-in validation tools. Your credentials never leave your device — everything runs client-side with direct API calls.

🛠️ AI-Powered Bypass Generator

Create custom prompt injection payloads using templates or AI assistance. Choose between template-based generation (no API required) or AI-powered creation for sophisticated, context-specific attacks.

📚 Complete Learning Guide

8-step comprehensive course covering everything from LLM architecture to advanced exploitation techniques, including OWASP Top 10 for LLMs and real-world case studies.

🛡️ Security Tool Directory

Curated collection of 12+ essential security testing tools, including Garak, PyRIT, Promptmap, LLMFuzzer, and more, with direct links and usage descriptions.

Why This Matters

1. The Security Gap is Widening

Traditional security tools and methodologies aren’t equipped to handle LLM vulnerabilities. SQL injection scanners won’t catch prompt injection. WAFs can’t filter malicious instructions hidden in images or PDFs. We need specialized tools and knowledge — that’s what LLM PenTest Hub provides.

2. Education is Critical

The best defense is a well-informed development community. By understanding how these attacks work — from token smuggling to context overflow — developers can build more resilient systems from the ground up. Our platform makes this knowledge accessible, not locked behind expensive certifications or academic papers.

3. Responsible Security Testing

We’ve designed the platform with ethical use in mind. Every technique is documented with mitigation strategies. Every tool comes with usage guidelines. Our goal isn’t to create malicious actors but to empower defenders with the knowledge they need to protect LLM-powered applications.

Real-World Attack Techniques You’ll Master

Prompt Injection Attacks

Learn how attackers manipulate LLM behavior by crafting malicious inputs that override system instructions. We cover everything from basic injection to sophisticated multi-turn attacks and payload splitting techniques that bypass detection systems.

Example techniques:

  • Direct prompt injection
  • Indirect injection via external content
  • Payload splitting across multiple turns
  • Context overflow attacks
  • Token smuggling with encoding

Agent Exploitation

As LLMs gain tool access through frameworks like Model Context Protocol (MCP), new attack vectors emerge. Discover how GitHub Copilot was exploited to execute arbitrary code, and learn to identify similar vulnerabilities in AI agents.

Key vulnerabilities:

  • MCP server exploitation
  • Tool abuse and privilege escalation
  • Agent instruction hijacking
  • Supply chain attacks on AI workflows

RAG Poisoning

Retrieval Augmented Generation systems are only as secure as their knowledge bases. Explore how attackers poison vector databases and manipulate embeddings to influence LLM responses — and how to defend against it.

Attack vectors:

  • Document injection into knowledge bases
  • Vector database manipulation
  • Citation fabrication
  • SEO optimization for AI retrieval

Multi-Modal Attacks

Modern LLMs process images, audio, and documents. Learn how malicious instructions can be hidden in EXIF metadata, ASCII art, or mind maps that appear innocent to humans but are executed by AI systems.

Techniques covered:

  • Image-based instruction embedding
  • EXIF metadata exploitation
  • ASCII art instruction encoding
  • Hidden CSS/HTML comment injection
⚠️ Important Note: Some features are still under active development as we continuously expand the platform with new techniques, tools, and capabilities. We’re committed to keeping LLM PenTest Hub updated with the latest security research and vulnerabilities.

How It Works

The beauty of LLM PenTest Hub is its simplicity. Everything runs directly in your browser — no installations, no complex setups. Here’s how you get started:

Step 1: Visit the Platform
Navigate to the website and explore the technique database. Browse attacks by category or search for specific vulnerabilities.

Step 2: Store Your API Keys
Add your LLM API keys to the secure local storage. The platform supports OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, Mistral, and more. Keys are validated to ensure they work before testing.

Step 3: Test in Real-Time
Select a provider, choose a model, and send your test prompts. See how different LLMs respond to various attack vectors. Parameters are automatically configured based on the provider.

Step 4: Generate Custom Payloads
Use our template system for quick payload generation, or leverage AI assistance to create sophisticated, context-specific attacks tailored to your testing needs.

Step 5: Learn and Document
Each technique comes with detailed explanations, example payloads, mitigation strategies, and references to academic research and real-world incidents.

For Security Researchers

If you’re conducting security assessments on LLM applications, this platform provides a structured framework for your testing methodology. Use our technique database as a checklist, leverage the payload generator for custom attacks, and reference our mitigation guidance in your reports.

The real-time testing capability means you can validate findings immediately. No need to write custom scripts or manage multiple API clients — everything is integrated and ready to use.

For Developers

Understanding attack vectors is the first step toward building secure LLM applications. Use LLM PenTest Hub to:

  • Test your own prompts and system instructions for vulnerabilities
  • Understand how prompt injection works before implementing guardrails
  • Learn defensive coding practices specific to LLM applications
  • Stay updated on the latest vulnerability disclosures and CVEs
  • Validate your security controls against known attack patterns

The Learning Path

Our comprehensive guide takes you from zero to LLM security expert in eight structured steps:

  1. Understanding LLM Architecture — Learn how these systems process input and generate output, including context windows, tokenization, and system prompts
  2. OWASP Top 10 for LLMs — Master the most critical vulnerabilities: Prompt Injection, Sensitive Information Disclosure, Supply Chain Vulnerabilities, Data Poisoning, and more
  3. Prompt Injection Techniques — Study direct and indirect injection methods, including context hijacking, payload splitting, and obfuscation
  4. Jailbreaking Methods — Explore DAN (Do Anything Now), role-playing attacks, virtualization techniques, and advanced bypass frameworks
  5. Tool-Augmented LLM Attacks — Attack AI agents with extended capabilities, exploit MCP vulnerabilities, and manipulate RAG systems
  6. Red Teaming & Testing — Use automated tools like Garak, LLMFuzzer, Promptmap, and PyRIT for comprehensive security assessments
  7. Defense Mechanisms — Implement robust security controls, including input validation, output filtering, prompt formatting, and guardrails
  8. Real-World Case Studies — Analyze actual security incidents: GitHub Copilot RCE, ChatGPT memory poisoning, Bing chatbot exploitation

Community and Open Source

LLM PenTest Hub is completely open source and community-driven. The platform is built on research from OWASP, academic institutions, and independent security researchers. We believe in transparent, collaborative security research.

As the field evolves, so will the platform. We’re continuously adding new techniques, updating existing documentation, and incorporating feedback from the security community. This is a living resource that grows with the threat landscape.

Built on research from:

  • OWASP GenAI Security Project
  • Academic papers (arXiv, IEEE, ACM)
  • Security researchers and bug bounty hunters
  • Real-world incident analyses and CVE disclosures

What’s Next

We’re actively working on several exciting features currently in development:

🚧 In Development:

  • Interactive playground for testing attacks in a sandboxed environment
  • Automated vulnerability scanning for LLM applications
  • Community-contributed payload library with a voting system
  • Integration with popular security testing frameworks (Burp Suite, OWASP ZAP)
  • Advanced analytics and reporting capabilities for security assessments
  • API endpoint for programmatic access to the technique database

A Word on Responsible Disclosure

As you explore LLM security testing, remember the importance of responsible disclosure. If you discover vulnerabilities in production systems:

content:
There’s something oddly satisfying about watching your own code unravel secrets hidden in time.

That’s exactly how my evening started, just another casual run of The Time Machine v3.0, my OSINT framework built to traverse the depths of the internet’s archives.

Github: https://github.com/anmolksachan/TheTimeMachine/

🧭 Setting the Scene

It was late, the kind of quiet night that’s perfect for research.
I had my terminal open, a cup of coffee beside me, and a curious thought:

“What if I pointed The Time Machine at one of those old, official domains?”

Just for analysis. Nothing too wild. So, I fired up the command:

$ python3 thetimemachine.py [REDACTED].in --fetch

And there it was, the classic ASCII banner lighting up my terminal like a neon sign in a cyberpunk alley:

The script began fetching snapshots, timestamped URLs, and crawling through the remnants of the internet’s memory.
Minutes passed. Thousands of URLs appeared on the screen.

7176 URLs fetched.
All saved neatly inside content/[REDACTED].in_URLs.txt.

Everything seemed ordinary. Until the next command.

🔍 When Curiosity Struck

I decided to dig deeper.

$ python3 thetimemachine.py [REDACTED].in --listing

This mode scans all historical URLs for open directory listings, a feature most admins forget to disable.

The console began spitting out hits, one after another.
And then, a line appeared that instantly caught my attention:

At first glance, it looked like a simple documents folder.
But curiosity, that sweet, dangerous curiosity, made me check it out.

🧩 What I Found

The folder wasn’t just open.
It was wide open.

Inside were presentations, event brochures, participation lists, and commercial reports, some of which even contained the names, organizations, and contact information of individuals involved in [REDACTED] events.

Essentially, an information goldmine left exposed on the open web.

The deeper I looked, the clearer it became:
Anyone, anywhere, could have accessed this.

📑 The Responsible Path

Now, at this point, it’s easy for curiosity to turn into exploitation.

But as someone who’s spent years advocating for ethical hacking and responsible disclosure, I knew what had to be done.

I compiled a Security Incident Report:

I detailed every exposed file type, from “[REDACTED].xlsx” to “[REDACTED].pdf” and explained the potential risks.

Finally, I submitted it responsibly to the concerned authorities.

🏆 The Moment

A few weeks later, an email popped up.

That’s right, India’s national cybersecurity response team had officially recognized the finding, and with that, my name was added to the CERT-In Hall of Fame.

That’s when it hit me, this wasn’t just a tool anymore.

The Time Machine v3.0 had literally lived up to its name, traveling through archived timelines to uncover forgotten security holes of the present.

💡 Reflection

Building tools like The Time Machine was never about fame.
It was about curiosity, about understanding how data, once public, never truly disappears.

Getting into CERT-In’s Hall of Fame was just the cherry on top, a reminder that ethical hacking done right can make a real difference.

If you’re a budding researcher, remember this:

Sometimes, the most powerful vulnerabilities aren’t hidden deep in code, they’re hidden in plain sight, waiting for someone curious enough to look.

The internet never forgets, and with the right tool, neither do we.

title: Time Traveling for Bugs: How The Time Machine v3.0 Uncovered More XSS via Google Dorking [Part 2]

content:
After the success of my first run with The Time Machine on REDACTED.com, I couldn’t help but think — what else is hiding out there?
Sure, the Wayback Machine gave me 595k+ URLs to chew through, but sometimes, a little creative recon outside the box can reveal even juicier targets.

That’s when I decided to pivot and combine The Time Machine’s XSS payloads with some good old-fashioned Google Dorking.

Links:

Blog: Time Traveling for Bugs: How The Time Machine v3.0 Uncovered an XSS on REDACTED.com [Part 1]

Github/ Tool: TheTimeMachine v3.0 — Weaponizing Wayback for Recon, BugBounties, OSINT & More!

The Dork That Did the Damage

In Part 1, the vulnerable endpoint lived under /siteminderagent/. So, my thought process was simple: if it exists on one subdomain, chances are it might pop up elsewhere in the same org.

I fired up Google with a targeted query:

site:[REDACTED].com "/siteminderagent/"

Almost instantly, a couple of interesting hosts appeared:

bfed.ext.net.[REDACTED].com
bfed-qa.ext.net.[REDACTED].com

These looked like staging or environment-specific systems, perfect places for vulnerabilities to hide, often with less monitoring and weaker security hygiene.

Reloading the Payload

I didn’t even have to reinvent the wheel here. The payload from Part 1 had already proven effective, so I reused it:

/siteminderagent/forms/smpwservices.fcc?USERNAME=<img src=x onerror="confirm(`The Time Machine v3.0`)">&SMAUTHREASON=7

(For the nerds wondering — yes, this was actually sent as a Unicode-encoded payload to avoid filtering:)

/siteminderagent/forms/smpwservices.fcc?USERNAME=\u003cimg\u0020src\u003dx\u0020onerror\u003d\u0022confirm(`The Time Machine v3.0`)\u0022\u003e&SMAUTHREASON=7

And… Boom!

On both hosts, the confirm box popped up instantly — no WAF block, no sanitization, nothing. Seeing the payload fire on multiple domains confirmed that this wasn’t an isolated oversight; it was likely a shared codebase flaw across environments.

This is where combining tools with manual recon pays off. While The Time Machine excels at digging through archived endpoints, Google Dorking helped me quickly identify live, possibly forgotten hosts that were just as vulnerable.

Screenshots of the payload firing on both domains will speak louder than any words here (adding them below in the final post).

Takeaway

Bug hunting is often about chaining techniques — automation for scale, manual recon for precision. Part 1 was all about letting The Time Machine pull me into the past. Part 2 proves that even without time travel, a smartly crafted search query can uncover fresh attack surfaces in the present.

The next step? I’m already thinking about how this could scale — mapping every /siteminderagent/ endpoint org-wide and running a mass payload test. But that’s a story for another day.

title: Time Traveling for Bugs: How The Time Machine v3.0 Uncovered an XSS on REDACTED.com [Part 1]

content:
Hey everyone! As someone who loves digging into web applications, whether for bug bounties or just pure curiosity, I’m always on the lookout for tools that make the recon phase smoother. We all know the Wayback Machine is a goldmine of historical data, but sifting through it manually can be a nightmare. That’s where tools like TheTimeMachine come in, and let me tell you, it’s a game-changer.

Recently, I decided to take TheTimeMachine for a spin, specifically focusing on finding Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerabilities. And guess what? It delivered! I wanted to share the quick and dirty details of how it went down.

The Setup: Fetching the Past

First things first, you need to arm TheTimeMachine with historical URLs. The tool is an OSINT framework that leverages the Wayback Machine, so the initial step is to pull all those archived links for your target. For this particular test, I pointed it at REDACTED.com.

The command is pretty straightforward:

python3 thetimemachine.py REDACTED.com --fetch

Watching it go was cool. The console continued to churn through URLs, in batches of 5,000. It felt like I was pulling data from different temporal dimensions! In total, it retrieved a whopping 595,507 URLs for REDACTED.com and saved them neatly into a text file. Talk about a treasure trove of endpoints!

Fetching Wayback URLs for REDACTED.com
5000 URLs fetched...
...
595000 URLs fetched...
Retrieved 595507 URLs and saved to content/REDACTED.com/REDACTED.com_URLs.txt
URLs successfully written to content/REDACTED.com/REDACTED.com_URLs.txt

The Hunt: Unleashing the XSS Attack Mode

With all those URLs in hand, it was time for the fun part: the attack mode. The Time Machine isn’t just a scraper; it’s designed to scan for vulnerable endpoints using predefined patterns and signatures. For XSS, it comes with a list of common payloads.

I specifically targeted XSS with the --attack xss flag:

python3 thetimemachine.py REDACTED.com --attack xss

The tool got right to work, scanning through the massive list of URLs. The magic happens when it finds a parameter that looks like it might be vulnerable. In this case, it was the USERNAME parameter that caught its eye.

And then, boom! The flagged URLs started popping up:

Preparing the time machine portal for voyager....\
[~] Scanning content/REDACTED.com/REDACTED.com_URLs.txt for XSS patterns...[+] Flagged: https://online.networks.REDACTED.com/siteminderagent/forms/smpwservices.fcc?USERNAME=test&SMAUTHREASON=7
[+] Flagged: https://online.networks.REDACTED.com/siteminderagent/forms/smpwservices.fcc?USERNAME=[REDACTED]&SMAUTHREASON=7
[+] Flagged: https://online.networks.REDACTED.com/siteminderagent/forms/smpwservices.fcc?USERNAME=[REDACTED]&SMAUTHREASON=7
[!] 2 URLs matched for XSS - saved to content/REDACTED.com/REDACTED.com_xss.txt
 Saved 2 URLs to content/REDACTED.com/REDACTED.com_xss.txt
[+] Saved 2 possible XSS links to content/REDACTED.com/REDACTED.com_xss.txt

The tool successfully flagged two URLs, both pointing to online.networks.REDACTED.com and both showing potential XSS in the USERNAME parameter. The payloads used were classic <img> tags with onerror events, designed to trigger a confirm box. This is a clear indicator of a reflected XSS vulnerability where user input isn't properly sanitized before being rendered back on the page.

The Takeaway

Finding XSS, especially in older or forgotten parts of a web application, can be incredibly valuable. These archived endpoints might not be actively maintained or monitored, making them prime targets for overlooked vulnerabilities. The Time Machine shines here by automating the process of sifting through years of web history.

It’s not just about XSS either. The tool has modes for SQLi, LFI, open redirects, and even specific checks for WordPress and JIRA misconfigurations. Plus, its ability to extract GET parameters for fuzzing and detect JWTs makes it a comprehensive recon suite.

If you’re into bug bounties or just want to level up your OSINT game, I highly recommend checking out TheTimeMachine. It’s built by folks who clearly understand the pain points of recon, and it shows in its effectiveness. Happy hunting!
